teenKit.tldr: In the 1960s, patients taking early antidepressants experienced terrifying, stroke-level blood pressure spikes after eating aged cheese and drinking wine. The culprit was tyramine, a natural compound that wreaks havoc when your body's chemical brakes are disabled by medication.
teenKit.whyItMatters: This historical medical mystery completely revolutionized how we understand drug-food interactions, proving that a single molecule can turn an everyday snack into a life-threatening crisis.
keyTakeaways: Early MAOI antidepressants blocked the enzymes meant to break down tyramine, causing a massive, dangerous surge in blood pressure.
Aged foods like cave-aged Stilton and sharp cheddar pack massive amounts of tyramine due to bacterial breakdown of proteins over time.
Popular culture blamed Chianti wine for decades, but modern clinical research exonerated bottled Chianti, proving the real danger lived in the cheese board.

vocab.meaning: A natural compound found in aged foods that can force blood vessels to constrict violently if it isn't broken down by enzymes in your gut.
An early class of antidepressants that work by disabling the enzymes responsible for clearing out certain brain chemicals and dietary amines.
A dangerous medical emergency where blood pressure spikes catastrophically high, risking stroke or organ damage.
The breakdown of proteins into smaller amino acids by bacteria and enzymes, which happens intensely during the aging of fine cheeses.

It was completely exonerated because bottled Chianti actually contains very low tyramine levels.
It was upgraded to being the sole cause of all 1960s medical crises.
It was proven to neutralize the effects of aged cheese.
